title: Advanced narrative and the future in the past
tagline: The plan didn't need to come true — that's exactly why English has a tense for it.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze (was/would/going/to)
Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (GOING, WOULD, HELD, START)
Writing Part 2 — story or article: sequencing a narrative with variety
Speaking Part 2 — recounting a personal anecdote vividly
why: Flat storytelling at B2 becomes layered storytelling at C1: a narrative that shows what had already happened, what was expected to happen, and what actually happened, sometimes in the same sentence. Examiners reward candidates who can narrate with this kind of depth in the Writing paper, and the historic present is exactly the shift that makes a spoken anecdote sound natural rather than rehearsed.

diagrams.title: A plan that never became real

marks.label: was going to move to Australia
marks.sub: future in the past: the plan at that time

diagrams.caption: The future in the past narrates an intention from inside the story — the timeline itself shows whether it came true.

rows.label: Meaning
cells: a past habit or state, now different

rows.label: Example
cells: Every winter we would ski in Huaraz.
The old printer wouldn't print in colour.

diagrams.title: Shifting into the historic present

before.text: Sofia opened the letter and immediately burst into tears.

after.text: Sofia opens the letter and immediately bursts into tears.

steps: Shift every main verb from the past simple to the present simple.
Keep any earlier, past-before-past event in the past perfect for contrast.
Use it only in spoken storytelling or a vivid passage — never across a whole formal narrative.

formula.chip: was/were going to · would · was/were to (have)
formula.ex: was going to leave / would leave / was to have left

formula.chip: a plan or arrangement, seen from a point in the past

head: Pattern
Meaning
Example
rows: an intention that may or may not have happened
was going to apply, but changed her mind
a later event in the story, viewed from an earlier point
Little did he know he would regret it
the ceremony was to begin at dawn
a plan that was cancelled or never completed
she was to have graduated that June
an activity in progress before another past event
had been raining for hours when we left
a past event narrated as if happening now, for drama

use.point: Past perfect continuous: the activity behind a past situation

examples.text: The pitch was waterlogged because it had been raining all night.
examples.note: the activity explains the later state

examples.text: Mateo was out of breath — he had been running to catch the bus.
examples.note: explains a past result, not just a fact

examples.text: By the time the ambulance arrived, the paramedics realised she had been lying there for over an hour.

use.point: Future in the past: was going to / would / was to (have) for plans that changed

examples.text: Nadia was going to study abroad, but the scholarship fell through at the last minute.
examples.note: was going to = a plan that didn't happen

examples.text: None of us realised that the quiet new student would become captain within a year.
examples.note: would = a later event, seen from the story's viewpoint

examples.text: The exchange programme was to have started in March, but it was postponed indefinitely.
examples.note: was to have + participle = a plan that was cancelled

use.point: Would for past habits vs wouldn't for refusal

examples.text: Every December, the whole family would travel down to the coast.
However hard Liam tried, the old laptop wouldn't connect to the network.
examples.note: refusal — common with machines, not just people

examples.text: As children, Sofia and her cousins would spend entire afternoons building sandcastles near Máncora.

use.point: Historic present for drama in spoken narrative

examples.text: So I'm sitting in the library, minding my own business, when suddenly the fire alarm goes off.
examples.note: historic present builds tension in a personal anecdote

examples.text: The final whistle blows, the crowd erupts, and Cusco has its first regional title in a decade.
examples.note: present tense narrating a decisive past moment

watch_out.wrong: I was going to called you, but I forgot.
watch_out.right: I was going to call you, but I forgot.
watch_out.why: Was going to is followed by the bare infinitive, never a past form.

watch_out.wrong: We would live in Trujillo when I was small, until we moved.
watch_out.right: We used to live in Trujillo when I was small, until we moved.
watch_out.why: Would doesn't normally describe a past state; use used to (or the past simple) for states.

watch_out.wrong: The door wouldn't opened however hard I pushed.
watch_out.right: The door wouldn't open however hard I pushed.
watch_out.why: After wouldn't (refusal), use the bare infinitive, not the past participle.

watch_out.wrong: He was to have finished the report, and in fact he finished it on time.
watch_out.right: He was to have finished the report, but in fact he never did.
watch_out.why: Was to have + participle implies the plan did not happen — don't use it for something that did.

watch_out.wrong: It has been raining for hours before we left, so the pitch was flooded.
watch_out.right: It had been raining for hours before we left, so the pitch was flooded.
watch_out.why: A past-before-past activity needs the past perfect continuous, not the present perfect.

watch_out.wrong: So he opens the door yesterday and sees the mess.
watch_out.right: So he opens the door and sees the mess.
watch_out.why: Historic present replaces the past tense entirely for that stretch — it never mixes with a past time marker like yesterday.

dialogue.title: The plan that changed
dialogue.context: Miss Vega asks Liam to recount his summer holiday using the historic present, and the story turns into an account of a trip that fell through.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Liam, you promised us a story about your summer. Go on, and try the historic present — make it dramatic.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Alright. So it's the last day of the holidays, and I'm at the airport, when suddenly my flight gets cancelled.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Wait, weren't you going to spend the summer in Chile with your cousins?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Exactly. I was going to stay there for six weeks, but the whole trip fell apart.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: My cousin had been planning the whole itinerary for months, and then her university offer changed everything.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: So you never went at all?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: No. The trip was to have started on the fifteenth, but it never did.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: And back at the airport — what did you do?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Well, I ring my mum, and she wouldn't answer the phone — she was still asleep.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Classic. Did anything good come out of it?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Actually, yes. As kids, my family would always go camping instead, so we did that — old habits die hard.

items.sentence: By the time we got to the stadium, the players ___ warming up for twenty minutes.
items.why: past perfect continuous: an activity in progress before another past event

items.sentence: I ___ hand in my project a day early, but my laptop crashed.
items.why: was going to = an intention that didn't happen

items.sentence: As a boy, my grandfather ___ walk two hours to school every day.
items.why: would for a repeated past habit

items.sentence: However many times I tried, the printer ___ connect to the network.
The two countries signed an agreement that ___ end the conflict, though peace took years to arrive.
items.why: was to + infinitive for a formal, fated arrangement

items.sentence: The ceremony ___ take place outdoors, but it was moved inside because of the storm.
items.why: was to have + participle for a plan that was cancelled

items.sentence: So I ___ down the corridor when I hear this strange noise behind me.
items.why: historic present narrates a past event as if it's happening now

summary: Future in the past (was going to, would, was to (have)) narrates a plan from inside the story, whether or not it actually happened.
The past perfect continuous shows the activity leading up to another past moment, not just the bare fact that it happened.
Would for a repeated habit needs an action verb; wouldn't for a refusal often describes people or machines.
Historic present drops the past tense for a stretch of spoken storytelling — it never mixes with past time markers like yesterday.
Was to have + participle always signals a plan that fell through.
